The challenge is the initial reduction from an arbitrary problem in NP to the problem you want to prove NP-complete.

In the usual approach, you assume a nondeterministic Turing machine (or equivalent) that solves the problem and a time bound (which can be an arbitrarily large polynomial). You then create a boolean expression that can be satisfied if and only if the Turing machine accepts the original problem instance. Unfortunately all constructions so far have included the time bound as a factor of the size of the expression.

Your formulation is a little bit exaggerated, but I (and many, though far from all, programmers) would agree with the following more "tame" formulation:

Getting software to solve a business problem in an elegant and maintainable way means that we got the abstractions right. Similarly, if a software can easily and elegantly be modified to cope with new business problems, it is also a strong sign that we got the abstractions right. In this sense, the business problems that the software solves are indeed just waypoints on the journey of finding the proper elegant abstractions for putting the business problems into code.

Turning these novel insights about "good" abstractions into code and programming languages enables the team to iterate faster and generate business value faster. So, appreciating that it indeed all about the journey means a commitment towards an approach to accelerate the rate with which the team can turn business insights into code and code into business value.

I know that many managers do hate such a formulation, but I stand behind it.

children.text:
One other thought, I think another aspect of biological sciences is just how much effort it takes to do research. Hypotheses are a dime a dozen, but actually verifying these is quite difficult. It takes a lot of patience, time, attention to details, and even then it often fails to replicate.

I don't think LLMs will just magically be able to connect all the dots, because "garbage in, garbage out" still applies. And there's just too many invisible intermediate states, there is literally just not enough information to fully constrain a model. Hence my interest in scaling computational chemistry to get these intermediates :)

To add to this I think there are “reductionist sciences” and “systems sciences”. Reductionist sciences are ones, like physics where there are lots of copies of a thing with near identical properties at different scales (the periodic table would be considered an incredibly short list and that seems to be one of the longest list of “different things” in physics).

Systems sciences are ones where each scale has lots of things with unique properties. If you think of “biological things between 2-4m” the amount of unique objects with unique properties and unique interactions is absolutely mind boggling. These sciences generally do not lend themselves to clean highly parsimonious models. The best you can do is coarse-grain a thing as a system (some very roughly defined set of interactions between different things) with certain behavior while accepting that you are losing enormous amounts of predictive power.

I suspect AI will remain worse at systems sciences for a long time because the “possible space” of models for a particular system is much larger than in the reductionist sciences and navigating it takes a human taste and instinct that LLMs don’t seem to have (yet).

Computational biochemistry is what I'm currently pursuing, but I'm pretty new to the field so take everything I say with a grain of salt: Biochemistry is a really really really tricky problem, for a couple reasons:

1. Biology has a very nasty habit of not cleanly abstracting. It's not like we can treat every protein as a "diffuse mass" without losing a ton of important interactions. This is unlike something like CFD where you can treat a mass of water molecules with certain constants. Think of something like cancer: a small mutation to a DNA strand can cascade into a tumor. You have to deal with the mutation happening at an atomic level while scaling to a whole organism (yes I know there's models that can approximate this, but they can't capture all the interactions).

2. This brings us to modelling at the atomic level. To model a system of atoms with the Schrödinger equation, it naively scales O(6^n) per particle. Note that means every nucleus and electron, so if you have say 10 carbon atoms and 22 hydrogen you're already at 10^127 operations. We can cut corners a bit and end up with something like CCSD which scales O(n^7), or cut more corners and scale O(n^3) for DFT. DFT is pretty much the last method where bond forming and breaking is modelled, so after more corner cutting you lose losing reactions, which are important for understanding why something is happening. Most protein folding simulations (moreso prior to alphafold) run a very crude approximation that models atoms as balls on springs (things like AMBER and CHARMM), which obviously can't handle reactions.

3. If this wasn't bad enough, you also can only move through time at about 1 femtosecond (10^-15), so it takes a ton of simulation steps to get even a nanosecond in. Forget millisecond or second lengths where things start to happen.

So, while the math of the physics exists, computationally it's practically intractible. There's some exciting work with something called Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIP) which approximate DFT using a neural network which are about 1000x faster than DFT, and iirc scale much more linearly (look at things like MACE and orbmol if you're curious). So we're making progress, but we've gone from so ridiculously impossible to pretty much impossible for large systems.

I have a couple ideas about developing custom microchips to make this faster, which is why I'm pursuing this, but there's still a massive way to go!

Ok my original comment was snarky (apologies to all three mods), but you've raised one of my favorite topics so I can't resist engaging a bit more seriously! In the second clause, that is -- the first is trivially true in some senses and trivially false in others, so it doesn't seem very productive to nail down.

So Chomsky thought of himself as a philosopher of science more than anything, and his life mission is/was to answer a fascinating question: what kind of creatures are we? There's been a growing consensus going back to at least Darwin that we're separated from the rest of Animalia by our "reason" (!= intuition != understanding != judgement != volition), but he helped popularize an old theory[1] that puts it kind of beautifully: human language is only possible in beings capable of producing an infinite set of meaningful outputs in response to a finite input.[2] And so far, that list includes only two definite members: Homo sapiens sapiens, and computer programs built upon large language models.[3]

So all that to say: yes, I think you're wrong; the programmatic ensembles that brought us today's breakthroughs are an "infinitely deep well". As long as we have questions to ask, they are not theoretically constrained from answering them.

Of course, this invites some obvious follow-ups on practicality; even the most impassioned ASI boomer wouldn't argue that the exact ensembles used here could answer every question in the universe. But A) that's possible because some infinities are bigger than others, and B) the exact same caveat applies to humans, whose cognitive capabilities are thoroughly determined by accidents of biology, culture, and episteme. The latter is the thrust of Chomsky's famous debate with Foucault, which is absolutely worth a watch for anyone who hasn't seen it (starting around ~18:00, AFAIR): https://youtu.be/3wfNl2L0Gf8?t=1080

---

TL;DR: I ultimately disagree on both points, yes. In the ways that matter, machines are no more constrained than animals.

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_von_Humboldt

[2]: Many animals are capable of communication, often quite complex and fascinating communication at that; even flora and fungi communicate! But language is qualitatively distinct. You may have heard this in the pithy-yet-mindbending sentiment "we've taught many apes to communicate with sign language, but none of them have ever asked a question."

[3]: It's no surprise in hindsight that trying to build better autocorrect got us to AGI; I find it unspeakably tragic that Chomsky never got the chance to see how thoroughly he's been vindicated, in this regard. Doesn't this make it seem like Wang had the wrong intuition, if her meyhod does not generalize? She proved Kakeya only in dimension 3, and also not prove the Hausdorff 3D Kakeya. In retrospect it seems humans were asking the wrong question, if a couple dozen pages long manuscript can subsume so many other efforts.

AI has only been able to advance the math frontier for a couple of months, fully grasping the applications, connections, and possible generalizations takes longer.

OpenAI's proof goes down a completely different route than the route taken for Kakeya in three dimensions and also the existing proof of local smoothing in two dimensions.

Hong Wang and Josh Zahl proved something a bit stronger, namely that the Kakeya conjecture holds for families of tubes satisfying the "Convex Wolff Axioms". From the outside this looks like a weird technical detail but if you unpack this you get an exceptional example of 'the journey is worth more than the destination'.

The idea for resolving Kakeya in R3 originates in the work of Jean Bourgain and a connection to the discretized sum-product phenomenon (the idea, in R, that "sum" and "product" are geometrically incompatible). This approach is summarized in Terry Tao's blog post from 12 years ago now [1].

Basically, the efforts to make this approach work resulted in the development of an entirely new and extraordinarily active subfield that one might call "continuous incidence geometry". This led to ideas like restricted projection theory (with spectacular applications in homogeneous dynamics and number theory), decoupling (another one of Thomas Wolff's ideas, and was realized by Bourgain and Demeter), the resolution of the Furstenberg set theorem, etc. There are very far-ranging applications, some of which even appeared on HN, and which a priori look totally unrelated, like the Heilbronn Triangle problem [2]

I know this is out of the context of most here on HN but let me say it in short: the development of the sum-product approach to Kakeya has resulted in a huge improvement of our understanding of the fundamental additive and multiplicative structure of Euclidean space.

OpenAI's proof of local smoothing in Rd shortcuts this entire matter. Don't get me wrong, the proof is phenomenal, and it's amazing that Local Smoothing admits a short, essentially self-contained proof (only uses some facts about elliptic PDEs which I can't comment about unfortunately since it isn't my area).

Hong Wang didn't win the fields medal for proving Kakeya in three dimensions (only). She won because of her incredible contributions to the development of continuous incidence geometry. The proof of local smoothing certainly contains a lot of very interesting insights into the wave equation but, if this proof had appeared in 2014 just like this, I do not think we would have had the same amount of development.

To me, this is the heart of the matter. For mathematicians, only having these incredible new proofs with no "social consequences" would be extraordinary. However, if we are not careful, the idea that math is "solved" will degrade the mathematics tradition in its own right. Where will be in 10 years, in 50 years? Humans, by virtue of being much worse at computations than computers, must build the "correct" abstractions in order to discover new mathematics. If this process is somehow lost, independently of the computer's ability to prove an infinite tower of new results, the mathematics tradition will suffer for it.

I asked Claude how will ETH being solved is a major breakthrough for mankind:

“ Honestly, nothing yet. This is a theoretical result, and it doesn't solve a real-world problem today.

*Why it won't change much in practice:* A running time like 2^(n/√log n) is "subexponential" on paper, but for real inputs it's still astronomically slow. For a few hundred variables it's no better than the brute-force methods we already have. Hidden constants in the exponent could also make it worse in practice. Real-world SAT solvers (the CDCL kind) already handle millions of variables on practical problems using heuristics, and this result doesn't replace them.

*Where SAT shows up in everyday life, indirectly:* - Verifying that chips (like the one in your phone) have no design bugs - Scheduling and logistics, like timetables, delivery routes, and airline crews - Software package dependency resolution - Security analysis and cryptography research

*What it could change over time:* - *Research direction:* Many problems were assumed to be hard because ETH says so. If ETH is false, researchers may find faster algorithms for them, and some of those could eventually matter in practice. - *Cryptography:* It doesn't break encryption, since the algorithm is still far too slow. But it could shift how people think about the hardness assumptions behind some security arguments. - *Theory of math and proof:* The Lean verification is also a notable example of AI-assisted, machine-checked mathematics.

So the "big deal" is mainly for computer scientists: a long-held belief about the limits of computation may be wrong. Any benefit to normal people would be long-term and indirect, and only if it leads to practical algorithms.“
